content: The PERCH study has generated numerous publications that detail its rationale, study design, and analytical methods, as well as preparatory analyses and sub-analyses. These resources are available for further review and reference. The economic burden of seasonal influenza, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), remains inadequately understood due to the lack of standardized cost analyses across nations. However, recent reviews indicate that direct costs associated with seasonal influenza are higher in high-income countries (HICs), while indirect costs are more significant in LMICs. These financial burdens disproportionately affect individuals who are least able to bear them. Vaccination is currently the most effective intervention for preventing and mitigating the impact of influenza. It also provides cost savings for countries. A review of over 140 studies revealed that the per capita cost of seasonal influenza cases ranges from USD $30 to over USD $60. The cost-effectiveness ratios for vaccination range from USD $10,000 per outcome to more than USD $50,000 per outcome. Influenza also exacerbates other global health threats, including noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), severe pneumonia, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). For instance, respiratory viral infections, including those caused by the influenza virus, have been shown to increase the risk of heart attack and stroke within three days of infection. Additionally, these infections frequently worsen chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Studies have also demonstrated that up to 50% of pneumonia cases are linked to respiratory viruses, and up to 45% of pneumonia cases in children involve viral-bacterial coinfections. Inappropriate use of antibiotics for viral respiratory infections, including influenza, continues to contribute to the growing problem of AMR. While more data are needed, there is already substantial evidence highlighting the relationships between influenza and these significant global health threats, which affect both HICs and LMICs. Investing in influenza prevention, control, and preparedness efforts yields secondary benefits that extend beyond influenza, strengthening health systems overall. Influenza impacts all countries, communities, and individuals. Seasonal influenza viruses will continue to circulate, and influenza viruses with pandemic potential will continue to emerge. This strategy serves as a global call for all countries and partners to prioritize the implementation of influenza programs as an investment in stronger health systems and pandemic preparedness. The Global Influenza Strategy 2019–2030 outlines high-level outcomes for 2030, including the development of better global tools and stronger country capacities. These tools and capacities aim to enhance research, innovation, and the availability of improved methods for the prevention, detection, control, and treatment of influenza. Every country is encouraged to establish a prioritized influenza program that is evidence-based, tailored to its specific needs, and contributes to both national and global preparedness, response, and health security. The strategy identifies four strategic objectives supported by ten priorities to achieve its vision and goals by 2030. These objectives include promoting research and innovation to address unmet public health needs, strengthening global influenza surveillance and data utilization, expanding seasonal influenza prevention and control policies, and enhancing pandemic preparedness and response. Promoting research and innovation involves advancing the development of novel diagnostics, vaccines, and treatments for influenza. This includes creating universal influenza vaccines with broader and longer-lasting immunity, developing more effective antiviral drugs and monoclonal antibodies, and improving diagnostic and surveillance methods such as next-generation sequencing and point-of-care testing. Operational research is also emphasized to optimize the use of current vaccines and antiviral drugs, assess newly approved technologies, and support regulatory authorities in expediting the approval of next-generation influenza products during emergencies. Strengthening global influenza surveillance and monitoring is critical for generating data that inform policy decisions. This includes enhancing integrated surveillance systems, expanding rapid risk assessment capabilities, and improving the understanding of influenza's impact and burden, particularly in LMICs. Effective communication strategies are essential for engaging policymakers and communities in prevention and control efforts. These strategies aim to increase understanding of influenza's risks and burdens, promote political commitment, and support the development of educational materials and risk communication plans. The WHO Secretariat plays a pivotal role in promoting research and innovation by developing focused plans, engaging funding and research partners, synthesizing evidence, and advocating for best practices. The strategy aligns with other WHO assets and initiatives, such as the Public Health Research Agenda for Influenza, the Global Action Plan for Influenza Vaccines, and the Research and Development Blueprint. By prioritizing influenza prevention, control, and preparedness, countries can reduce the burden of seasonal influenza, minimize the risk of zoonotic influenza, and mitigate the impact of pandemic influenza. These efforts contribute to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and improving global health security.
